tracks.title: One word in front of a title
tracks.text: Lesson 04 point 6 — to-dos. This one is a deep dive, under org… the grammar. And the whole idea fits in a sentence. A to-do is a headline whose first word is a state. [curious] One keyword, standing in front of a title. There is no board database anywhere in this ecosystem. [excited] Re-running the file is resuming. Moving a word is the transition. And git diff is the audit trail. The org lesson named these states in passing — native, not convention. This page is the full grammar behind that one chip.

tracks.title: State lives in silos
tracks.text: First — state lives in silos. Every agent system reinvents task state… and every reinvention buries it somewhere nobody can read. A JSON queue here. A status column there. A mark-done API over there. Three shapes for the same idea — and the state always ends up in a database the human can't diff and the agent can't be audited on. [sighs] And done, in those systems, is the thinnest fact of all. A boolean somebody set. Not a claim that was checked… not a state that survives a restart… just a flag flipped by whoever held the write token. [sarcastic] Trust the silo. Hope the silo is right. Here's the trouble. Agents need state both sides can read. The model needs to see where the work stands. The human needs to see what the model did. A column in a vendor's cloud satisfies neither. The format that's legible to both already exists — and it's older than all of this.

tracks.title: The definition
tracks.text: The definition. A to-do is a headline whose first word is a state. One keyword in front of a title — read by the engine as the task's position in its own state machine. The outline is the machine. The keyword is the interpreter's only input. That's the entire mechanism. Org already had the grammar — a keyword standing in front of a headline — and Workbooks runs it literally. The engine's whole state model is six words before a title. No board schema… no status table… no second copy. One module is the engine of record, and its own description puts it in five words. The outline IS the state machine.

tracks.title: The state words
tracks.text: Now — the state words. The default set is six active words and three done words. The active ones, in order. First, TODO — queued, not started. Second, NEXT — the pick-up signal. Third, WAITING — blocked on something outside. Fourth, DOING. Fifth, STARTED — both meaning in flight. And sixth, BLOCKED — held, after a crash or an unmet edge. Then the done side, three of them — DONE… CANCELLED… and the American spelling, CANCELED. How does the engine pick the state? The simplest rule there is. Take the first word of the headline after the stars. If it's in the set, that's the state. If it isn't, the word just stays in the title. Position alone. [curious] And you can replace the whole set with one line. A hash-plus-TODO line swaps the keywords out. The editorial board for bit-ml does exactly this — its own pipeline stages, ASSIGNED, RESEARCH, WRITING, EDIT… and then PUBLISHED and KILLED. But here's the honest catch. The divider between active and done is cosmetic to this engine. The done-side is hard-coded — DONE, CANCELLED, CANCELED, and nothing else. So a custom done word like PUBLISHED is a state the engine recognizes… but it is not a done-state. It won't get skipped on resume the way a real DONE does. Invent states freely for selection. Just know that finished — stop touching it — is spelled exactly three ways.

tracks.title: Who moves the word
tracks.text: Next — who moves the word. Start with what the engine does not do. It never rewrites your file's keywords. There is no write-back code in the run path. A run reads your outline, executes the leaves, and lands its results in telemetry. Your headlines stay exactly as you wrote them. Moving a keyword is the author's edit — or an agent's — made in a commit. The transition is a git diff, every time. Now picture the life of one task as a graph. It starts at TODO — parked. A dream verdict, or you, promotes it to NEXT — the pick-up signal. An agent claims it by writing its name on the node and committing… and to every peer, a claimed task goes invisible. The claim turns it DOING. A run that passes the gate lands it on DONE, in green. But a crash or a timeout drops it to BLOCKED — never a stuck DOING. And from either active state, a dream can route the task to CANCELLED, the grey terminus. Every single edge is labeled by an actor… because state never moves on its own. [curious] Even the machine obeys this. The dreaming process emits verdicts, and the engine applies them by exact heading match. Pick up writes NEXT. Put down writes TODO. Cancel writes CANCELLED. Even the dreamer moves state through the proper keywords — never by hand-picking out of band. [chuckles] There is one place keywords appear without a human — the generated mirrors, TASKS dot org and BOARD dot org. But those are one-way renders, drawn from a ledger, not synced. And when the runtime reboots, orphan-correction rewrites any stale DOING or TODO to BLOCKED. A crash becomes a held task you can see… never a lie about active work.

tracks.title: What a run does with states
tracks.text: What a run does with states. When the engine runs the outline, it walks each heading and asks a few small questions. Follow the tree. First question — is this heading already a done-state? If yes, it's skipped, and recorded as DONE with the output, already DONE. And that one fact is what makes a run resumable. Re-running the same outline picks up exactly where it left off, because finished work is simply passed over. A cancelled task in the file even normalizes to DONE in the record — abandoned still counts as settled. If it's not done, second question — does it have children? A leaf — no children — runs its work, and reaches DONE if its validation passes… else FAILED. A composite — a heading with children — reaches DONE only if all of its children ended DONE… else PARTIAL. So the run-result vocabulary is exactly three words. DONE… FAILED… PARTIAL. Two properties shape how children run. Ordered, set to true, makes them sequential — a pipeline. Its absence makes them parallel — eight wide, with a thirty-minute ceiling per task. And blocker is an explicit wait edge — this task holds until that one is done. One last thing, and it surprises people. [curious] Every heading is a node. There is no task-tag filter. A heading with no keyword and no children still runs as a leaf. So if you post a raw board with a star-log heading… the log heading runs too. Boards meant to be rendered are not the same shape as outlines meant to be run.

tracks.title: What DONE actually records
tracks.text: What DONE actually records. This is a depth rung — skippable — but it's where DONE stops being a feeling and becomes a row. The engine never edits your file. What it produces is a record per task, and each record has exactly six fields. First — id, the title slugged: lowercased, non-letters turned to dashes, capped at forty-eight characters. Second — idx, the position in the run. Third — title, the headline with the keyword stripped. Fourth — state, one of DONE, FAILED, or PARTIAL. Fifth — output, the agent's result, truncated to six hundred characters. And sixth — ts, unix seconds when it settled. [curious] The quiet detail — id keys off the title, not the position. State follows the words, not the line number. Reorder your headlines and the same task keeps its identity. Which is also why a run resumes cleanly across edits — the engine recognizes a task by who it is… not where it sits.

tracks.title: DONE is a claim until checked
tracks.text: DONE is a claim until checked. A leaf reaches DONE only if its validation passes — and that gate is the whole difference between a boolean somebody set and a fact something proved. The gate is a done-when property, or a check block in the body. It runs in the WASM shell — over the command registry, never native bash — and it's fail-closed. The engine only believes a pass if it sees the sentinel… a specific magic string in the output. No sentinel, no DONE. And if there's no check at all? The agent's own completion stands. Which means a no-check DONE is the agent grading its own homework. That's an honest limit, not a bug — and it has its own full lesson, validations, which walks the whole done-when ladder. The one-line version. DONE is only as trustworthy as the check behind it.

tracks.title: How a change becomes history
tracks.text: How a change becomes history. A state change doesn't vanish into a database. It falls onto three rails at once — each readable by a different audience. Picture the path of one keyword-move, from an agent's edit to a signed ledger. Rail one — git. The protocol is to record by moving state, never deleting, in the same commit, plus one dated line under a star-log heading. The git log is the board's memory. Rail two — telemetry. Every run persists to a telemetry database — a task-events table holding each record, and a step-events table ingested from an always-on steps file… every tool call the agent made, logged at the chokepoint. Rail three — the sealed ledger. At the end of every run, the engine hash-chains the raw lines of that steps file. Each hash is the sha-256 of the previous hash joined with the next raw line — starting from a fixed genesis string. Then it signs the head with the tenant's did-key. Verify returns two properties — tamper-evident… and attributable. Anchor commits the ledger back into the tenant's repo. The full seal, verify, and anchor story is its own page — the ledger. Here, we only show the hop from a state… to its history.

tracks.title: Reading the record
tracks.text: Reading the record. Another depth rung. The morning after a run, three verbs answer three questions — what ran, what broke, and whether anyone edited the story. First — what ran. Type wb telemetry, and you get a runs index. One line per run, with its stage, its call count, its error count, and total milliseconds. Second — what broke. Type wb telemetry, then the slug, and you get that one run's detail — stage, calls, errors, and a line per failed step, like step seventeen, bash, exit one. Third — prove nobody edited the story. Type wb ledger, then the slug. It re-walks the hash chain and confirms the head still matches its signature. The reply reads tamper-evident ok, attributable ok, the count, and the did-key. [whispers] If a single byte of history were altered… tamper-evident would not say ok. And over HTTP it's the same record, live. Post to the workflow endpoint with your org text, you get back a slug, and you poll a status file for per-task stages — running, done, or error.

tracks.title: Where it bites
tracks.text: Now the honest part — where it bites. [sighs] Four sharp edges. First — the divider is cosmetic. The bar in a hash-TODO line is decoration to the run engine. The done-set is hard-coded. Custom done keywords are selectable states… not skip-on-resume states. Second — two parsers disagree. The Elixir workflow engine knows the full keyword set. But the kernel — the wb query command — uses orgize with its default config, which only knows TODO and DONE. So wb query reports state only for literal TODO and DONE. A NEXT or DOING stays inside the title there. Same file… two vocabularies. Know which one you're asking. Third — every heading is a node. There's no task filter. Post a raw board and your star-log heading runs as a leaf like everything else. Fourth — a no-check DONE is self-grading. Without a done-when, the agent's word is the only evidence. The autopoet hit this honesty-gate directly — a self-report of completion is a hypothesis, not a result, until something independent confirms it. And one more, a feature really — orphans become BLOCKED. A crash mid-run leaves a stale active state, and on boot the groundskeeper rewrites it to BLOCKED. By design, a crash becomes a held task you can see… never a stuck DOING that lies.

tracks.title: Questions people actually ask
tracks.text: Quick fire. Can I invent my own states? Yes — for selection. A hash-TODO line replaces the whole set, and agents can claim work through your custom stages. But done-detection stays DONE, CANCELLED, CANCELED. Does the engine update my file? No. No write-back code at all. Results land in telemetry and the ledger — your headlines stay as you wrote them. Which is exactly why the git diff is the audit trail. What's the difference from beads? Two ledgers, never crossed. Beads is the issue tracker, with its own database. The to-do grammar is state in the plan file itself, with git as history. Rendered mirrors can draw from beads, but that's a one-way render… not a sync. Is DONE trustworthy? [curious] Only as strong as its gate. A DONE with a passing check, run fail-closed in the WASM shell, is a proven fact. A DONE with no check is the agent grading its own homework. Same word… different evidence. And — why does wb query miss my NEXT tasks? Because it's the kernel parser, not the workflow engine. orgize's default config only knows TODO and DONE. The Elixir runner knows the full set. Same file… two vocabularies.

tracks.title: Back up to org
tracks.text: So that's to-dos. A headline whose first word is a state — and an outline that IS the state machine. No board database. Moving a word is the transition. Git diff is the audit. [curious] The way back up is short. This deep dive sits under org — lesson 04 — the grammar that makes the plan parseable at all. And it reaches sideways to two more — validations, for the done-when ladder that decides what DONE can mean… and the ledger, for the full seal, verify, and anchor story. But the parent is org. Everything here is just six words… standing in front of a title.
